data.section: The Manor, Peasants and Village Life
data.sourceTitle: Manors, Villeins and the Farming Year
data.targetTitle: Manors, Villeins and the Farming Year
data.sourcePassage:
Most people in medieval England did not live in castles or fight in famous battles. They lived in villages, worked on farms, attended church, paid rents and obeyed local rules. The manor was one of the most important units of rural life — an estate controlled by a lord that included land, buildings, courts and rights.

Peasants were not all the same. Villeins were tied to the manor: they owed labour services, paid rent and had to use the lord's mill. They could not leave without permission. Freemen had more legal independence, could move more freely and could take disputes to different courts. Landless labourers owned nothing and worked for wages, making them especially vulnerable when harvests failed.

Farming was central to village life. In many villages, land was divided into open fields, with each family holding strips scattered in different areas. This system spread risk — if one area flooded, a family might still harvest from other strips. The farming year shaped everything: ploughing and sowing in spring, haymaking and harvest in summer, and slaughtering animals and storing food before winter.

Daily food was simple for most peasants: pottage, coarse bread, peas, beans and ale. Meat was less common. Peasant homes were small, with timber frames and thatched roofs. Medieval people also enjoyed leisure — religious festivals, fairs, games and seasonal celebrations gave moments of rest and community, though life was shaped by hard work, disease and the constant fear of a bad harvest.

questions.question: What was a villein?
options: A wealthy landowner who controlled a manor
A peasant tied to the manor who owed labour services and rent to the lord
A town merchant who traded in wool
A Church official who collected tithes
questions.modelAnswer: A villein was a peasant legally tied to the manor, who owed labour services, paid rent and could not leave without the lord's permission.

questions.question: Why did the strip farming system spread strips across different parts of the field?
options: So that lords could control exactly how much each family produced
To spread risk so that if one area had poor soil or flooding a family might still harvest from other strips
Because strips were distributed by lottery each year
To make it easier for stewards to count the amount of land farmed
questions.modelAnswer: Strips were scattered across the field to spread risk. If one area was flooded or had poor soil, a family might still harvest successfully from other strips.

questions.question: How was a freeman different from a villein?
options: Freemen were wealthier than lords
Freemen owed more labour services than villeins
Freemen had more legal independence and could move more freely and use different courts
Freemen owned no land at all
questions.modelAnswer: Freemen had more legal independence than villeins. They could move more freely, take disputes to different courts and were not tied to the manor in the same way.

questions.question: The passage says medieval people 'also enjoyed leisure'. Why is it important to mention this in a study of medieval life?
options: It shows that medieval people worked less than modern people
It challenges an oversimplified view of medieval life as only hardship by showing that ordinary people had community, celebration and rest
It proves that poverty had no effect on medieval people
It shows that the Church banned all forms of hard work
questions.modelAnswer: Mentioning leisure challenges a simple view of medieval life as nothing but misery and hard work. It shows that ordinary people had community activities, festivals and celebrations, giving a more rounded picture of their lives.

data.sourcePassage:
Towns grew in medieval England, especially from the 1100s onwards. They were still small by modern standards but were important centres of trade, craft and local government. Towns grew because farming produced goods to sell, kings and lords granted market rights, trade routes developed and merchants brought distant goods to local buyers.

Guilds were central to town life. A guild was an organisation of people in the same trade or group of merchants. Guilds set training rules, controlled who could join a trade, inspected goods and punished poor workmanship. They also supported sick members and organised religious events. An apprentice lived with a master for several years, learning the trade in exchange for work and obedience. After training, an apprentice could become a journeyman, working for wages, and eventually a master if accepted into the guild.

Towns also faced serious problems. Streets were narrow and crowded. Waste from households, butchers, tanners and animals could end up in lanes and rivers. Fire was a constant risk because buildings were timber and thatch and workshops used ovens and furnaces. Town authorities made rules about cleaning streets, waste disposal and fire, but enforcement was difficult.

For some people, towns offered escape. A villein who lived in a town for long enough could sometimes claim greater freedom. Women could sell goods, run businesses and continue a trade as a widow. Jewish communities contributed to town life through trade and finance, but faced legal restrictions, heavy taxation and persecution. Merchants who prospered could become wealthy and influential, funding churches, guilds and local affairs.

questions.question: What was a guild?
options: A type of market held once a year at a cathedral
An organisation of people in the same trade that controlled training, standards and membership
A legal document granting a town the right to hold a market
A system of taxation used by lords to control craftspeople
questions.modelAnswer: A guild was an organisation of people in the same trade or group of merchants that set training rules, controlled membership and inspected goods.

questions.question: Why was fire a particular danger in medieval towns?
options: Medieval towns banned the use of water to put out fires
Buildings were made of timber and thatch, and workshops used ovens and furnaces
Medieval fire fighters were poorly trained and refused to work
Towns were always built on land prone to drought
questions.modelAnswer: Buildings in medieval towns were made of timber and thatch. Workshops used ovens, furnaces and candles. A small fire could spread rapidly through closely packed buildings.

questions.question: What path did an apprentice follow to become a master craftsman?
options: Apprentice → master → journeyman
Journeyman → master → apprentice
Apprentice → journeyman → master
Master → journeyman → apprentice
questions.modelAnswer: An apprentice trained with a master, then became a journeyman working for wages, and could eventually become a master if accepted into the guild.

questions.question: The passage describes towns as offering 'escape' for some people. What does this suggest about medieval social mobility?
options: Medieval society was completely rigid with no possibility of social change
There were some routes by which people could improve their legal status or opportunities, even if movement was limited
Anyone in medieval England could freely move between towns at any time
Towns offered no opportunities that were not available in villages
questions.modelAnswer: The passage suggests that medieval society, while hierarchical and restrictive, was not completely fixed. Villeins could gain freedom in towns, women could run businesses, and merchants could rise to wealth and influence, showing limited but real possibilities for social mobility.

data.sourceTitle: The Black Death, Peasants and Change
data.targetTitle: The Black Death, Peasants and Change
data.sourcePassage:
Medieval life faced repeated crises. The Great Famine of 1315-1317 caused harvest failures, widespread hunger and death. Then, in 1348-1349, the Black Death reached England and killed a large proportion of the population. These disasters showed how vulnerable medieval communities were to disease and harvest failure.

The Black Death changed labour relations. When large numbers of workers died, labour became scarce. Some surviving peasants and labourers found they could demand higher wages. Lords and the government tried to resist this through the Statute of Labourers in 1351, which tried to hold wages at pre-plague levels. Tension over taxation, labour laws and social hierarchy eventually contributed to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381, when thousands of ordinary people marched on London.

The condition of Jewish communities in medieval England also showed how vulnerable minorities could be. Jewish people had lived in English towns since the Norman Conquest. They contributed to trade and finance but faced legal restrictions, heavy taxation and false accusations. In 1190, Jewish people in York were massacred. In 1218 they were ordered to wear a badge. In 1290, Edward I expelled all Jewish people from England.

Despite crises and changes, much continued. Farming remained central. Social hierarchy persisted. Religion shaped daily life throughout the period. Women continued to face legal and social limits. Change was real — towns grew, some peasants gained more freedom, and labour relations shifted after the plague — but it was slow and uneven. Many ordinary people still faced hard work, disease and social control.

questions.question: What was the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
options: A rebellion by French peasants against English rule
An uprising by ordinary people protesting against taxation, labour laws and social hierarchy
A revolt by merchants against guild control
A military campaign by lords against the king
questions.modelAnswer: The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 was an uprising in which thousands of ordinary people marched on London to protest against taxation, labour laws and social hierarchy.

questions.question: How did the Black Death change wages and labour relations?
options: It reduced wages because so many peasants were desperate for work
It had no effect on wages because plague did not affect farm workers
It created labour scarcity, allowing some workers to demand higher wages
It caused all peasants to be given their freedom by the king
questions.modelAnswer: The Black Death killed large numbers of workers. With labour scarce, some surviving peasants and labourers could demand higher wages from lords who needed workers.

questions.question: What happened to Jewish communities in England in 1290?
options: They were granted full legal equality with Christians
They were expelled from England by Edward I
They were forced to move to London and forbidden to live in other towns
They were required to convert to Christianity
questions.modelAnswer: In 1290 Edward I expelled all Jewish people from England. This followed a long period of persecution including massacres, legal restrictions and forced badge-wearing.

questions.question: The passage describes both change and continuity in medieval England. Which is the best description of this relationship?
options: Medieval England changed completely and quickly after the Black Death
Medieval England never changed in any way throughout the period
Change existed but was slow and uneven, while many core features of society persisted
The Black Death ended all forms of social hierarchy permanently
questions.modelAnswer: The passage shows that while important changes occurred — such as labour relations shifting after the plague, towns growing and some peasants gaining more freedom — core features like social hierarchy, farming and religious life persisted. Change was real but slow and uneven.
